newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive - Peters the power broker.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive - Peters the power broker.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Sept 24 - Winston Peters, "fading into the sunset", is a long shot to become prime minister after next month's general election in New Zealand, Forbes magazine writer Steve Hanke suggests.

But becoming prime minister in the first post-MMP coalition government is not what the charismatic New Zealand First leader is realistically aiming for -- even though his rhetoric may suggest otherwise.

Instead, Peters' objective is to be the power broker in the next parliament. That's where he wants NZ First to position itself, right in the centre, able to call the shots whether Labour or National is the dominant party.
He sees himself playing the role the Free Democrats have done for more than 20 years in German politics.
Peters has got where he has by scratching every visible (and invisible) itch in the body politic.

He has, on several key issues, modified his policy, as he himself admitted on nationwide television at the weekend, in the face of evidence that his original stand, or programme, was too extreme or unworkable.
That pragmatism in itself does not bother his followers, who perceive him to be the only man of principle in New Zealand politics.
He has attacked, with equal vigour, National, Labour, the Alliance, the Christian Coalition and ACT.
There are great risks for NZ First if it is seen to be identifying with either National or Labour, at this stage.

Peters could lose those voters who chose Labour in 1993 but have since deserted in the ratio of two-to-five to NZ First, and he could also push away those whose primary objective is the defeat of the Bolger-led government.

In refusing to be pinned down on whether he would work in coalition with Labour or National, he seeks to scoop up the votes from the disenchanted from both the Right and the Left -- and at the same time leave himself room for manoeuvre in the post-election coalition deal making.
He has, too, made it clear that any party who wants his support will have to pay a high price.
National, for example, would have to sacrifice Jim Bolger, Bill Birch and Jenny Shipley, if it wanted to govern with NZ First backing.
And Labour would have to accept his compulsory superannuation scheme, event though it knows that the eight cents in the dollar forced savings would hit workers hardest.
As power broker, Peters could demand key portfolios, as the Free Democrats have done in Germany.

And, in exchange for his support on issues of confidence, he could insist the governing party accept his priority policies. At the same time he could blame the governing party for anything that went wrong.

The spectre that hangs over New Zealand First is the capacity of the smaller parties -- particularly ACT and the Christian Coalition -- to cross the five percent threshold and secure enough seats to shut New Zealand First out of its power-broking role.
Hence his increasing virulent attacks on those he calls the "toxic trio": National, ACT and the Christian Coalition.

According to the latest NZ Herald-Waikato University election poll, the most widely touted coalition government -- of NZ First and Labour -- has declined in attraction to NZ First voters during the first week of the campaign, though among Labour supporters the prospect has increased in appeal.

Among those who intend voting for NZ First, Labour and the Alliance -- groups roughly equal in number -- NZ First people would prefer coalition with the Alliance, Labour people would prefer the Alliance, and Alliance supporters return the compliment.
The poll suggests that NZ First voters are less well disposed to Labour than they were before the campaign began.
Twenty-eight percent preferred Labour then; only 24 percent did last week, less than the 30 percent for coalition with the Alliance.
But still fewer NZ First people, 14 percent, down from 19.5 percent the previous week, welcomed coalition with National.
The question is whether the anti-National forces will be ultimately self-defeating. What is becoming increasingly plain is that they might be unable to form a viable governing coalition.
